what_it_does: Computing-in-memory (CIM) chips — chips that do math directly inside the memory array rather than shipping data to a separate processor — are organized as multiple cores, each containing a grid of tiny resistive cells (called a crossbar array) that can multiply numbers in place. Deploying a neural network (specifically a convolutional neural network, or CNN — a model that processes images through layers of sliding-window filters) onto such a chip requires deciding which weights go into which core's crossbar and in what order to execute each layer, because poor assignment wastes crossbar capacity and causes cores to wait on each other. This paper proposes two linked strategies: a weight-mapping strategy that fills crossbar arrays more fully for CNNs, and a scheduling strategy based on streaming data through cores in a pipeline — like an assembly line — so that handoffs between cores overlap with computation and reduce idle time. The novelty is treating the mapping and scheduling problems together in the context of flash-memory-based (eFlash) CIM chips, which have specific capacity and timing constraints not addressed by prior work.
